name: Skin flooding

lead: Skin flooding is a social-media skincare routine in which several thin layers of water-attracting (humectant) products, such as glycerin or hyaluronic-acid serums, are applied to damp skin and then covered with a moisturizer. People use it for a hydrated, bouncier, less flaky look.

The routine is built on ordinary moisturizer science: humectants draw water into the outer skin layer and occlusives slow its loss. Research on the specific multi-layer routine is limited, though the individual ingredient categories are well described.

paras: Practitioners cleanse, leave the skin slightly damp, apply light hydrating layers one after another, and finish with a cream or occlusive to seal in water. It is typically done at night, sometimes combined with a gentle mask.

Humectants can pull water out of deeper layers if not sealed with an occlusive, and some users report stinging with humectant-rich products. Layering many products raises the chance of irritation or reaction to individual ingredients.

angle.text: Better-hydrated outer skin can look smoother and less flaky, which is the look people aim for with skin flooding. It is done with ordinary hydrating products.

lead: Skin flooding is a skincare routine popularised on social media in which thin layers of hydrating, humectant-based products are applied to damp skin and then sealed with a moisturizer. People use it to make skin look more hydrated, plump and smooth.

It relies on a basic distinction in moisturizer chemistry. Humectants such as glycerin attract water into the stratum corneum, while occlusives such as petrolatum reduce water loss from the surface [1][2]. Layering the two is the standard way moisturizers are described as working.
No published trial has tested skin flooding as a named routine. Research on moisturizers shows some benefit in atopic dermatitis, with no single type clearly better than others [2].
infobox: Humectants (e.g. glycerin), occlusive or cream to seal

paras: The routine layers hydrating products in thin coats, usually starting from the lightest and finishing with a richer cream or occlusive. Humectants include glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol, butylene glycol, urea and lactic acid, with glycerin among the most popular cosmetic humectants [1].

Humectants attract water to the stratum corneum [1]. Moisturizer references describe humectants as pulling moisture from humid air or deeper skin layers, which is why they are usually paired with occlusives; a petrolatum layer can cut water loss by 50 to 75 percent for several hours [2]. Applying products to damp skin is a practitioners' step intended to give humectants water to hold; moisturizer references reviewed do not specifically address it.
No studies found on skin flooding as a routine. Studies of moisturizers in general show some benefit for atopic dermatitis, improving comfort and possibly reducing flares [2].
Some users of humectant-rich treatments have reported smarting and stinging [1]. Humectants without an occlusive can leave deeper layers drier [2].
